en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Twenty, Chapter on Mātaṅga.
4. The Sirīmantajātaka:
“One endowed with wisdom but devoid of fortune, or one possessed of fame but lacking wisdom;”
I ask you this matter, Senaka:
what do those skilled in these things say is better here?
"Both the wise and the foolish, O Lord of Men..."
Those possessed of craft and those without craft,
those of noble birth and those of low birth,
even the famous become the servants of others.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
'One who is deficient in wisdom, though possessed of beauty, is indeed superior.
I ask you too, O one of matchless wisdom:"
Mahosadha, who sees only the Dhamma, asks:
"Between a famous fool and a wise man with no wealth, which of these is better?
Those skilled in the Dhamma declare."
“The fool commits evil deeds,
thinking, ‘This world alone is better’;
he sees this world but does not see the world beyond.”
In both cases, the fool took hold of misfortune;
having seen this as well, I declare:
wisdom is better than being merely renowned as a fool.
“Neither craft, nor kinship, nor physical beauty brings wealth;
but one who is blind and mute may thrive in happiness.”
For Fortune indeed attends him as she does a great bull;
seeing this too, I say that one who possesses fortune is better than one who is deficient in wisdom.
“One of little wisdom becomes intoxicated when obtaining pleasure,
and even when touched by pain, he falls into delusion; being touched by adventitious pleasure and pain, [he is led astray].”
He trembles like a water-dweller in the heat;
having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom is better, not the fame-seeking fool.
"Just as birds from all directions flock together toward a mango tree in the forest laden with sweet fruit,
even so do people gather around one who is wealthy, possessing riches and enjoyments."
The majority of people associate for the sake of their own interest;
having seen this as well,
I say that one who possesses wisdom is better than one who merely possesses glory.
“It is not good for a powerful fool to acquire wealth through violence;
this witless man will only cry out in distress.”
They drag one down to the terrible hell;
having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better, not the fame of a fool.
“Whatever rivers flow into the Ganges,
they all abandon their names and lineages;
when the Ganges reaches the ocean, [they too become the sea].”
Even wisdom is not seen to possess such power as this in the world;
having observed this as well,
I say that one who is deficient in wisdom is better than one who possesses mere glory.
“Into this great ocean which they call the deep,
into which all rivers flow incessantly and in incalculable numbers,
the sea always possesses a surging force.”
The great ocean does not exceed its shore;
even so, the longings of a fool never surpass his wisdom in glory.
Having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better, not the fame of a fool.
Even if one who is unrestrained works for the welfare of others...
The illustrious one who speaks while seated in the assembly—
that very speech bears fruit for him in the midst of his kinsmen;
for it is glory that makes him so, not wisdom.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
one who possesses wisdom, even if lacking in worldly splendor, is better than one who is merely glorious.
Whether for the sake of another or for oneself,"
The fool of little wisdom speaks falsely;
he is censured in the midst of the assembly,
and later he goes to a state of misery.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better than a man of mere renown who is a fool.
Even if one of vast wisdom speaks what is true,"
One who is debt-ridden, without property, and poor— his [desire] does not flourish in the midst of kinsmen;
for one who lacks wisdom, there is no prosperity.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
one who possesses wisdom, even if lacking in worldly splendor, is better than one who is merely glorious.
Whether for the sake of another or for oneself,"
The one of vast wisdom does not speak falsehood;
he is honored in the midst of the assembly,
and in the end, he goes to a happy destination.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better than a famous fool.
Elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings—"
And women born into wealthy families—
all these become objects of enjoyment for a man of prosperity who lacks such prosperity himself.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
one who is wise but lacking in prosperity is better than one who possesses prosperity but is deficient in wisdom.
"One whose actions are not well-ordered..."
Fortune abandons the foolish person who speaks foolishly,
just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better, not the fame of a fool.
"We five are wise, O Blessed One."
All stand with palms joined in reverence;
you are our sovereign, surpassing all,
like Sakka, the lord of beings and king of the gods.
"Having seen this as well, I say:
one who is wise is better than even one who possesses glory but lacks wisdom.
A fool, though famous, is like a slave to the wise man."
When such matters have arisen,
that which the wise man discerns with subtlety,
therein the fool falls into delusion.
Having seen this as well, I say:
wisdom alone is better than a man of renown who is foolish.
Indeed, wisdom is always praised by the virtuous.
People are devoted to sensual pleasures and wealth;
yet the wisdom of the Buddhas is of incomparable nature,
for glory never surpasses wisdom.
“What we asked, you have explained to us,
O Mahosadha, seer of the complete Dhamma:
a thousand cows, a bull, and an elephant.”
"And these ten chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses;
pleased by your answer to my question,
I give you sixteen excellent villages."
The Sirīmantajātaka, the fourth.
